claim: Chromosome compaction is essential for reliable transmission of genetic information.
source: Chromosome compaction is essential for reliable transmission of genetic information.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws from established scientific knowledge about chromosome biology.

claim: Experiments suggest that ∼1000-fold compaction is driven by condensin complexes that extrude chromatin loops.
source: Experiments suggest that ∼1000-fold compaction is driven by condensin complexes that extrude chromatin loops, by progressively collecting chromatin fiber from one or both sides of the complex to form a growing loop.
evidence: This statement references experimental observations about condensin-driven compaction, though specific citations are not provided in this sentence.

claim: Theory indicates that symmetric two-sided loop extrusion can achieve such compaction.
source: Theory indicates that symmetric two-sided loop extrusion can achieve such compaction
evidence: This refers to theoretical predictions from prior work.

claim: Recent single-molecule studies observed diverse dynamics of condensins that perform one-sided, symmetric two-sided, and asymmetric two-sided extrusion.

evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Golfier et al., 2020.

claim: High compaction can be achieved if even a small fraction of condensins have two essential properties: a long residence time and the ability to perform two-sided (not necessarily symmetric) extrusion.
source: High compaction can be achieved if even a small fraction of condensins have two essential properties: a long residence time and the ability to perform two-sided (not necessarily symmetric) extrusion.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the simulations and theory presented in the manuscript.

claim: In mixtures of condensins I and II, coupling two-sided extrusion and stable chromatin binding by condensin II promotes compaction.
source: In mixtures of condensins I and II, coupling two-sided extrusion and stable chromatin binding by condensin II promotes compaction.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: During mitosis in metazoan cells, each chromosome is linearly compacted ~1000-fold from a ~1-mm-long chromatin polymer globule into a ~1 µm array of chromatin loops.
source: During mitosis in metazoan cells, each chromosome is linearly compacted ~1000-fold from a ~1-mm-long chromatin polymer globule into a ~1 µm array of chromatin loops (Paulson and Laemmli, 1977; Marsden and Laemmli, 1979; Earnshaw and Laemmli, 1983; Maeshima et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: This remarkable reorganization is primarily driven by the protein complex condensin.
source: This remarkable reorganization is primarily driven by the protein complex condensin (Hirano and Mitchison, 1994; Saitoh et al., 1994; Saka et al., 1994; Strunnikov et al., 1995; Hirano et al., 1997; Shintomi et al., 2015; Gibcus et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Condensin is one of a class of DNA-binding complexes known as structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes.
source: which is one of a class of DNA-binding complexes known as structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC) complexes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about condensin classification.

claim: Condensin is believed to compact the chromatin fiber by an active process known as 'loop extrusion'.
source: Condensin is believed to compact the chromatin fiber by an active process known as 'loop extrusion' (Yatskevich et al., 2019; Banigan and Mirny, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In the loop extrusion model, a loop-extruding factor (LEF), such as a condensin motor, binds the chromosome and progressively grows a DNA/chromatin loop by translocating along and processively collecting the nearby chromatin fiber.
source: In the loop extrusion model, a loop-extruding factor (LEF), such as a condensin motor, binds the chromosome and progressively grows a DNA/chromatin loop by translocating along and processively collecting the nearby chromatin fiber (Riggs, 1990; Alipour and Marko, 2012; Goloborodko et al., 2016b).
evidence: This describes the loop extrusion model with supporting citations.

claim: DNA loop extrusion by condensins and other SMC complexes has recently been observed in single-molecule experiments in vitro.
source: DNA loop extrusion by condensins (Ganji et al., 2018; Golfier et al., 2020; Kong et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020) and other SMC complexes (Kim et al., 2019; Davidson et al., 2019; Golfier et al., 2020) has recently been observed in single-molecule experiments in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: It has not been established how condensins with the properties observed in vitro can attain the high degree of linear compaction required for mitotic chromosome compaction in vivo.
source: However, it has not been established how condensins with the properties observed in vitro can attain the high degree of linear compaction required for mitotic chromosome compaction in vivo.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge that the manuscript addresses.

claim: In the first single-molecule experiments that directly imaged loop extrusion, yeast condensins were observed to extrude DNA loops in an asymmetric, 'one-sided' manner.

claim: In one-sided loop extrusion, part of the condensin complex remains anchored to DNA, while condensin extrudes DNA from one side of the complex into a loop.
source: In this mode of loop extrusion, part of the condensin complex remains anchored to DNA (Kschonsak et al., 2017), while condensin extrudes DNA from one side of the complex into a loop (i.e., collecting DNA either upstream or downstream of the bound site, but not both) (Ganji et al., 2018).

claim: One-sided extrusion contrasts with most models for loop extrusion by condensin, in which each loop-extruding factor performs symmetric 'two-sided' extrusion.

evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental observations and simulation results.

claim: Dimerization could facilitate two-sided extrusion by combining two one-sided complexes, while also stabilizing binding of condensin II to DNA by increasing the condensin-DNA binding surface.
source: Dimerization could facilitate two-sided extrusion by combining two one-sided complexes, while also stabilizing binding of condensin II to DNA by increasing (or otherwise modifying) the condensin-DNA binding surface.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about molecular mechanisms.

claim: This combination of effects would naturally generate a tight coupling between two-sided extrusion and long residence times.
source: This combination of effects would naturally generate a tight coupling between two-sided extrusion and long residence times.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about molecular mechanisms.

claim: Dimerization could simultaneously allow two-sided extrusion and increase the residence time, generating the necessary conditions for chromosome compaction by mixtures of one- and two-sided condensins.
source: Thus, dimerization could simultaneously allow two-sided extrusion and increase the residence time. This combination would generate the necessary conditions for chromosome compaction by mixtures of one- and two-sided condensins.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion about molecular mechanisms.

claim: Metazoan chromosomes are composed of large (~400 kb) chromatin loops with condensin II at their bases, with smaller (~80 kb) loops mediated by condensin I nested within.
source: Metazoan chromosomes are composed of large (~400 kb) chromatin loops with condensin II at their bases, with smaller (~80 kb) loops mediated by condensin I nested within (Gibcus et al., 2018; Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental studies with citations.

claim: Condensin II is tightly localized to the central axis of the rod-like chromosome, while condensin I is localized along the axis in a broader pattern.
source: Consequently, condensin II is tightly localized to the central axis of the rod-like chromosome, while condensin I is localized along the axis in a broader pattern (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi et al., 2017; Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental studies with citations.

claim: This hierarchy of loop nesting naturally emerges from the loop extrusion model for mixtures of LEFs with two different residence times.
source: This hierarchy of loop nesting naturally emerges from the loop extrusion model for mixtures of LEFs with two different residence times.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: In 3D, the bases of these loops localize along a central axis.
source: In 3D, the bases of these loops localize along a central axis (Goloborodko et al., 2016a; Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a result from prior modeling studies with citations.

claim: This hierarchy emerges in mixtures of LEFs with the properties of condensins I and II, mixtures of one- and two-sided LEFs, mixtures of two populations of one-sided LEFs, and mixtures of two populations of two-sided LEFs.
source: This hierarchy emerges in mixtures of LEFs with the properties of condensins I and II (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), mixtures of one- and two-sided LEFs (Figure 2b, bottom left), mixtures of two populations of one-sided LEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 4e), and mixtures of two populations of two-sided LEFs (Gibcus et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations with references to figures and a citation.

claim: Not all combinations of LEF symmetries and dynamics can fully compact mitotic chromosomes (two-sided extrusion is required).
source: While not all combinations of LEF symmetries and dynamics can fully compact mitotic chromosomes (two-sided extrusion is required; Figure 4)

claim: Differences in residence times can generate the nesting structure required for the patterns of spatial localization of condensins I and II observed in vivo.

evidence: This is a conclusion from the simulation results.

claim: The residence time of condensin II in vivo is longer than that of condensin I.
source: Consistent with this idea, the residence time of condensin II in vivo is longer than that of condensin I (Gerlich et al., 2006a; Walther et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an observation from experimental studies with citations.

claim: Mitotic chromosome morphology can be controlled by the relative ratio of condensin I to condensin II.
source: Previously, it was shown that mitotic chromosome morphology can be controlled by the relative ratio of condensin I to condensin II (Shintomi and Hirano, 2011).

claim: Condensin II is responsible for lengthwise 'axial' compaction along the central axis of a chromatid, while condensin I drives 'lateral' compaction, reducing the width of a chromatid.
source: Generally, condensin II is responsible for lengthwise 'axial' compaction along the central axis of a chromatid, while condensin I drives 'lateral' compaction, reducing the width of a chromatid (Ono et al., 2003; Shintomi and Hirano, 2011; Green et al., 2012; Bakhrebah et al., 2015; Shintomi et al., 2017; Hirano, 2016; Kalitsis et al., 2017).

claim: Morphology and the degree of linear compaction could be controlled by the relative residence times of condensins I and II and the fraction of condensins that perform one-sided extrusion.

claim: A perturbation that increases the residence time of condensin II could lead to greater lengthwise compaction due to the larger loops that would be formed by condensin II.

source: In the loop extrusion model, LEFs can linearly compact chromosomes by extruding chromatin into loops within approximately one LEF residence time.
